title: Whiteboarding LLD Diagrams in Interviews
summary: The practical, time-boxed version of UML that actually gets used in a live interview — legible shorthand over textbook-perfect notation.

slides.markdown:
Textbook UML has dozens of notation rules; a live interview gives you five to ten minutes and a shrinking whiteboard. Whiteboarding LLD (low-level design) is the compressed dialect that actually gets used — boxes, arrows, and three relationship types, drawn fast enough to leave time for the conversation.

This topic is about the practical shorthand and the time-management skill around it: what to draw, what to skip, and how to keep talking while your hand keeps moving.

slides.sectionTitle: What interviewers actually expect: legible shorthand, not textbook-perfect UML
slides.markdown:
No interviewer is grading whether your diamond is exactly 6mm wide or whether you remembered the `~` package-private marker. What they're actually watching for is whether your boxes and arrows are *consistent* — the same shape always means the same relationship — and whether the diagram matches what you're saying out loud.

A common miscalibration goes the other way too: skipping notation entirely and drawing undifferentiated boxes connected by plain lines loses the one thing a diagram is for — showing *what kind* of relationship each connection is. The bar is "a stranger could read this back correctly," not "this would pass a UML certification exam."

slides.sectionTitle: A practical shorthand: boxes, arrows, and the 3 relationship types you actually need
slides.markdown:
In a real interview, three relationship types cover almost every design: a plain line for **association** ("these two know about each other"), an open-diamond line for **has-a with independent lifecycle** (aggregation), and a hollow-triangle line for **is-a** (inheritance, collapsing inheritance and realization into one arrow unless the distinction is specifically asked about). Composition's filled diamond is worth keeping too, but only reach for it when lifecycle ownership is actually the point being tested.

Skip multiplicities unless the interviewer's question hinges on cardinality — writing `1` and `0..*` next to every single line adds ink without adding signal in a fast whiteboard sketch. Add them back the moment the conversation turns to "can this be zero?"

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a real interview-paced whiteboard sketch for a parking lot's core classes
slides.markdown:
This is roughly what you'd actually produce in the first three minutes of a "design a parking lot" question — not a polished diagram, a working sketch.

```
ParkingLot ◆── Level ◆── ParkingSpot

Vehicle (abstract)
   △
   ├── Car
   └── Motorcycle

ParkingSpot --- Vehicle   (a spot holds at most one vehicle)
```

Notice what's missing on purpose: no attributes, no method signatures, no multiplicities beyond what's written in parentheses. `ParkingLot` owns `Level`s and `Level`s own `ParkingSpot`s (composition — a spot doesn't exist outside a level), while `Vehicle` is a small inheritance hierarchy off to the side. That's enough structure to start a real conversation about allocation logic.

slides.sectionTitle: Sequencing the interview: when to sketch classes vs when to talk
slides.markdown:
A useful default split: spend the first few minutes sketching the core classes and their relationships in near-silence (narrating briefly, not explaining every line), then switch to talking through behavior, edge cases, and trade-offs once the skeleton is up. Trying to fully narrate every box as you draw it slows the sketch down and often means you never finish it.

Watch for the interviewer's own signal — if they start asking questions before you've finished sketching, stop drawing and answer; the diagram is a tool to enable the conversation, not a deliverable that has to be completed before discussion starts.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: over-formatting the diagram and running out of time to code
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "A cleaner, more complete diagram — perfectly ruled boxes, every attribute typed, every multiplicity labeled — makes a stronger impression."

**Why it's wrong:** LLD interviews almost always expect you to get to actual code before time runs out. An interviewer who watches you spend twelve minutes perfecting a diagram, leaving eight minutes to write code for a design that took twelve minutes to draw, reasonably concludes you can't prioritize under a deadline — which is itself part of what's being evaluated.

**Correct model:** treat the diagram as a five-minute scaffold, not the deliverable. Rough boxes, the right relationship types, minimal labels — then move to code, where you can still refine the design as you go.

slides.sectionTitle: Talking while drawing: narrating decisions as you sketch
slides.markdown:
Silent drawing reads as uncertainty even when you know exactly what you're doing. Narrate the *decisions*, not the mechanics — "I'm making `Vehicle` abstract since we'll never instantiate one directly" is useful; "now I'm drawing a box" is not.

A good rhythm: state the class you're about to add and why it exists, draw it, then name the relationship as you connect it — "`ParkingSpot` and `Vehicle` are just associated, not owned, since a spot can sit empty." This turns a silent sketch into a running commentary the interviewer can follow and interrupt at any point, which is exactly what makes the diagram collaborative instead of a solo exercise they watch.
